SUBJECT:  WORKSHOP  ON  CALIFORNIA  ENVIRONMENTAL  QUALITY  ACT
(CEQA)

PURPOSE:  To  provide  the  Plaru'iing  Commission  with  an  overview  of  the  California
Environmental  Quality  Act  (CEQA).

BACKGRO'[mD:
The Planning  Commission  requested  this workshop  at a previous  meeting  to better  understand  the
requirements  of  CEQA.  Occasional  trainings  on topics  such  as CEQA  will  help  the Planning
Commission  make  informed  decisions  on upcoming  projects  and help educate  the public  on issues
being  discussed.  Furthermore,  the  workshop  provides  an opportunity  for  staff  to update  the
Plaru'iing  Commission  and priblic  on new laws taking  effect.

In response  to  the growing  public  concern  over  the environmental  damage  caused  by industrial
expansion  and  the  lack  of  clear  federal  policy  on  environmental  protection,  the  National
Environmental  Policy  Act  (NEPA)  was passed  in 1960  and signed  into  law on January  1, 1970.
NEPA  requires  federal  agencies  to consider  the environmental  impact  of their  actions  before  they
make  a decision.  NEPA  mandates  that  federal  agencies  thoroughly  assess the  environmental
effects  of  their  proposed  actions  and  engage  the  public.  Similarly,  in  response  to  NEPA,
California's  legislature  passed  the California  Environmental  Quality  Act  (CEQA)  and signed  it
into  law  in  1970.  The  law  requires  agencies  to  disclose,  analyze,  and  mitigate  potential
environmental  effects,  such  as impacts  on  air  and  water  quality,  before  approving  projects.
Additionally,  CEQA  encourages  public  participation  and coordination  among  state, regional,  and
local  agencies  Since  its enactment,  CEQA  has continued  to be modified  by new  legislation  and
shaped by case  law.

New  Laws  Affecting  CEQA
In 2018,  CEQA  underwent  a comprehensive  update  to its implementing  guidelines.  Notably,  the
update  incorporated  amendments  mandated  by Senate  Bill  743, transitioning  the primary  metric
for transportation  impact  analysis  from  the traditional  measure  of traffic  congestion  (Level  of
Service,  or LOS)  to Vehicle  Miles  Traveled  (VMT).  This shift was intended  to align  CEQA  review
with  state goals  of promoting  sustainable  land use patterns  and reducing  greenhouse  gas emissions.
The  ripdated  guidelines  also  provided  enhanced  direction  for  the  analysis  of  climate  change
impacts,  including  assessing  a project's  contribution  to greenhouse  gas emissions.  The  overall
amendment  clarified  the CEQA  process  by incorporating  recent  legislative  changes  and relevant
court  decisions,  adding  detail  to existing  exemptions,  and refining  the environmental  checklist
rised for initial  studies.

  3
 In June 2025, the Governor signed into law Assembly Bill 130 and Senate Bill 131, reforming the
California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA). These reforms were aimed at expediting housing
production and infrastructure development throughout the state. These amendments, which took
immediate effect, created a new statutory CEQA exemption for qualifying urban infill housing
projects, streamlining the approval process by reducing permitting times and limiting opportunities
for litigation. The reforms also included additional CEQA exemptions for a range of projects,
including certain types of infrastructure and community facilities. These changes represent a
significant policy shift away from more extensive CEQA review for certain projects, with the
intent of facilitating faster project approval, particularly in urban infill areas.

CONCLUSION:
Staff will provide a presentation to the Planning Commission to discuss the California
Environmental Quality Act (CEQA).

 CEQA AT A GLANCE
 • California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA)
 • Signed into law in 1970, modeled from the National
  Environmental Policy Act (NEPA)
 • Informs decision-makers and the public about potential
  environmental effects of proposed activities
 • Encourages public participation and coordination among state,
  regional, and local agencies
 • Statewide environmental protections for over 50 years

Recent Changes to CEQA
 • Recent amendments as of June 2025
  •  Creating new exemptions
  •  Limiting litigation risk
  •  Streamlining reviews
 • Last comprehensive update was in December 2018
  •  CEQA in reverse
  •  Levels to Service (LOS) to Vehicle Miles Traveled (VMT)

  7
 Recent Changes to CEQA
 • California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA)
 • Signed into law in 1970, modeled from the National
  Environmental Policy Act (NEPA)
 • Informs decision-makers and the public about potential
  environmental effects of proposed activities
 • Encourages public participation and coordination among state,
  regional, and local agencies
 • Statewide environmental protections for over 50 years

What It Is
 • California law: enacted in 1970 to protect the environment
  from potential harm caused by development projects.
 • An informational tool: an environmental review process that
  identifies potential impacts on the environment and proposed
  mitigation measures to reduce or eliminate those impacts.
 • A decision-making framework: a framework to weigh the
  environmental consequences of a project against its economic
  and social benefits before deciding on whether to approve it.
 • Public participation: an opportunity for public involvement in
  the environmental review process that allows individuals and
  organizations to comment on projects and their potential
  impacts.

  8
 What It Isn’t
•  Project Veto: CEQA does not automatically stop projects from being
  built; it is intended to inform decision-making, rather than grant or
  deny entitlements.
•  Stand-alone approval process: CEQA is separate from approvals
  required for a project (e.g., conditional use permit). CEQA does not
  guarantee project approval even if environmental impacts are
  adequately mitigated.
•  Guarantee of a perfect environment: CEQA strives to minimize
  environmental impacts, but it cannot eliminate them entirely.
•  Obstacle to development: While CEQA adds a layer of complexity to
  projects, its intended purpose is not to act as an obstacle but rather to
  promote responsible and sustainable development through informed
  decision-making, mitigation measures, and public engagement.

When CEQA Applies
  • Projects, defined as: an activity which may cause either a
  direct physical change in the environment, or a reasonably
  foreseeable indirect physical change in the environment,
  and which is any of the following:
  a) An activity directly undertaken by any public agency.
  b) An activity which is supported in whole or in part, through
  contracts, grants, subsidies, loans, or other forms of assistance
  from one or more public agencies.
  c) An activity that involves the issuance to a person of a lease,
  permit, license, certificate, or other entitlement for use by one
  or more public agencies.

 • Balance CEQA and Project Review
